text:
Predicates:
SchedulesMeeting(x, y) ::: x schedules a meeting with y.
GoToCompanyToday(x) ::: x will go to the company today.
HasLunchInCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company.
HasLunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorksRemotelyFromHome(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
InOtherCountries(x) ::: x works in other countries.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
James ::: the individual James.

Premises:
∀x (SchedulesMeeting(x, y) → GoToCompanyToday(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (HasLunchInCompany(x) → SchedulesMeeting(x, y)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (HasLunchInCompany(x) ∨ HasLunchAtHome(x)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x (HasLunchAtHome(x) → WorksRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountries(x) → WorksRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
¬Manager(x) ∧ ¬InOtherCountries(x) → ¬WorksRemotelyFromHome(x) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
James ↔ (Manager(James)) ::: James will appear in the company today if and only if he is a manager.

Conclusion:
(Manager(James) ∨ InOtherCountries(James)) → ¬(HasLunchAtHome(James) ∨ WorksRemotelyFromHome(James)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(HasLunchAtHome(James) ∨ WorksRemotelyFromHome(James)) → ¬(Manager(James) ∨ InOtherCountries(James)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
